Changelog

How Lion got here

Every release since Apr 6, 2026, with each change it shipped and each decision it made, in the words of the commits and notes that say so. Lion writes this page itself from a model of its own development kept beside its code: 4627 claims, each a source's words and what they say, in history/notes. Which release shipped what is worked out from git, not written down.

37 findings wait for a decision

Rules over the model find where the project disagrees with itself. Each finding is evidence against something the project assumes, and stays listed in history/research/known.json until a decision or a fix settles it.

12Against Lion behaves as every rule in force predicts
  • AGENTS.md says not to commit proof into git (a7c2a88), yet 38d9144 committed proof videos after it, and two are still in the repository: packages/repl/artifacts/thicker-black-background-dots.webm and .artifacts/proof/repl-server-output-dock.webm. Settle by deleting them.
  • An empty string counts as false in a cond (README, probe), where Scheme counts every string as true. Part of cond's JavaScript truthiness: see cond-zero-condition.
  • cond counts a condition as JavaScript does: false, null, 0, and "" are false (README, probes), where Scheme counts only #f as false. Filters, by contrast, require true or false (filter-truthiness). No decision covers cond's truthiness.
  • The vendored typesafe-ai skill (fa4cab8) says to keep API credentials server-side in web apps; the editor's Jev playground (af779dc) keeps the user's key in tab memory and sends it through a proxy. Third-party advice; settle with a decision that says why the playground differs, or withdraw the rule.
  • e888677 stated that functions given too few arguments return a curried function; fc4959c made quote and eval with no arguments fail and rewrote the tests, still named 'should return a curried function', to expect the error. No commit withdraws the rule. Settle with a decision that withdraws it.
  • DESIGN.md said the system is 'crease-first and lightly lifted' (a564abc), while 532cfda and ba16c89 made node shadows weighty. Fixed in the working tree: packages/repl/DESIGN.md now says what can be manipulated is lifted with weight. It clears once the commit that fixes it is read into the notes.
  • e888677 held that every value is JSON, and fc4959c let a host function's undefined through. No later commit says what a host function returning undefined gives; a decision or a probe with a host function would settle it.
  • A lambda ignores extra arguments 'as in JavaScript' (c771be4, 356e74a, README), so host code can call it as a callback; Scheme raises an error. Decided (lambda-arity) but never named as an exception to the Scheme rule, and the arity rule lists it as its own exception.
  • e888677 stated that functions given too few arguments return a curried function; fc4959c made quote and eval with no arguments fail and rewrote the tests, still named 'should return a curried function', to expect the error. No commit withdraws the rule. Settle with a decision that withdraws it.
  • The record score-improves-past-noise and the lion-reasoning SKILL.md say that another run of an earlier version "can only raise what came before, which takes an improvement back". On the skill's own core, what a version is sure to give is its worst run, so another run of a version that already has one leaves a later improvement as it was, or makes it larger; a probe that adds a better run of the earlier version finds the improvement kept. The sentence holds only for the first run of an earlier version that had none. Found on 2026-11-16 by the probe of the case. Settle by rewording the record and SKILL.md, or by changing the rule.
  • 4c8df1b's message says a belief is judged from the version it was formed in, but the plain model in reasoning-skill.test.ts says other beliefs are judged in the present; the mutation list treats judging only in the present as a break, so the test comment looks stale.
  • Same departure as the unbound-string conflict: Lion returns the string, Scheme raises an error. Settle with a decision that lists Lion's departures from Scheme as exceptions.
3Against Where Lion follows a precedent for a behavior, the precedent is Scheme, Racket, or JSON, or JavaScript for a library function that mirrors a JavaScript operation
  • Lambdas ignore extra arguments 'as in JavaScript' (356e74a): a base form following JavaScript, not Scheme. See lambda-extra-arguments.
  • The arity-rule decision record says a lambda ignores arguments past its parameters as JavaScript does, so host code can call it as a callback; a Scheme lambda refuses them. A decision that keeps this departure would settle it with an exception to scheme-racket-semantics.
  • The README says arguments beyond a lambda's parameters are ignored 'as in JavaScript'. See lambda-extra-arguments.

  2. Nov 182026

    @lionlang/core 0.14.1 @lionlang/cli 0.13.1

    No invariant refuses a change that assuming only assumes: an invariant keeps the database, and an assumed change does not change it. In 0.14.0 an invariant whose filter asked with assuming could hold of different facts depending on whether it was declared before them or after, and one whose assuming added a new fact for each answer never finished. Now it holds of the same facts in any order and never asks itself again.

  3. Nov 182026

    @lionlang/core 0.14.0 @lionlang/cli 0.13.0

    Plain code is compiled to JavaScript functions and runs 9 to 25 times faster, and a call in tail position keeps nothing of the call it is in, so a loop runs in constant memory. ["assuming", change, ..., expression] asks what would hold after a change and leaves the database as it is. schema/open names the rest of a record or list, and a keyed relation can declare "merge", a lattice aggregate that joins the values its key gets. When a key or an equality rule makes values one, the value kept is their least, so answers no longer depend on the order of rules or facts; this is a breaking change, as is host code that read a scope's bindings through a Ref. A group whose rules invent unknowns follows a change to facts one component of values at a time, and a schema whose lambda asks about itself no longer runs Lion out of memory. Research runs share one Lion model in research/.

    @lionlang/core 0.13.0 @lionlang/cli 0.12.0

    why explains a fact that does not hold as well as one that does: each rule that could have given it, the goals of its body that held, and what stopped it. It returned null before, so this is a breaking change. It marks with "assumed": true what could change once an unknown is known, and it shows the same derivation whatever order the facts arrived in. The lion-reasoning skill records what each experiment was expected to fix, and what is carried to a new score.

    • 20 Changed
    • 5 Decided
    • 7 Rules

    Added 7

      Added why-derives-followed-group-again capabilityRecord why tells the derivation a new database finds firstwhy-tells-first-derivation.json
    • The lion-reasoning skill records what each experiment was expected to fix, and says whether it did. A direction's notes list the problems it addresses, and a belief that tries a direction, such as {"id": "collapse-1", "tries": "collapse", "predicts": [{"question": {"case": "double spaces", "suite": "titles"}, "value": "pass"}]}, is what one experiment of it was expected to do, judged in the version it was recorded in and no other. Where it predicts a problem's question otherwise than the problem shows, the experiment targets the problem, which is fixed or unfixed by what that version answers. carried lists the directions whose experiments say nothing about a score, because none ran it with an earlier version to beat, as when the same eval is run under another model or a new benchmark arrives. Three standing questions ask what each experiment was expected to fix and whether it did, which problems still show though every direction that addresses them is set aside, and which directions are carried to a score. bun run skill-eval prints the models that ran each run, as models: claude-opus-5-5, so a run's model can be part of the score's question.

    @lionlang/core 0.12.0 @lionlang/cli 0.11.0

    The logic layer grows with its facts. What rules derive is kept and follows every change to the facts and the rules, in a full database and in a goal-directed query, instead of being derived again from nothing. A join runs in batches and keeps far less in memory, and a load under invariants or schemas no longer reads every row again for each form.

It covers loading facts one form at a time and many, with invariants, schemas, and keys; asking every row and one; rules that join, aggregate, negate, and recurse; and changing a fact and asking again.     @lionlang/core 0.11.0 @lionlang/cli 0.10.0

    Rules that say something exists without saying what it is. A rule can give every person a mother nobody has named, and the value it invents is ordinary Lion data that a program can write, store, compare, and look up. Keys and equality rules make two such values one, and a goal-directed query shares what full evaluation has derived.

    • exists and some are names of special forms, so a relation, a define, or a lambda parameter can no longer be named "exists" or "some".

    • It is a breaking change: why no longer returns null for a fact that does not hold

    Added 57

    • exists in a rule head says the head holds for values nobody has given, and the rule invents them: ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], ["person", "?c"]] gives every person a mother. A rule invents only for an answer whose head does not hold already, so with ["mother", "ada", "eve"] it invents nothing for ada. Rules that invent wait until every rule that invents nothing has finished; then every rule that invents, and whose head does not hold, invents, all at once; the other rules run on what was invented; and so on until nothing more is invented. So the result does not depend on the order rules or facts were added in. A rule that invents cannot aggregate: ... both aggregates and lists variables in "exists". A rule that invents values cannot aggregate.
      Added existential-rules capability Added exists special-form786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • A rule head can be an and of relation calls, which adds a row to each: ["rule", ["and", ["p", "?x"], ["q", "?x"]], ["r", "?x"]]. Under exists, one unknown is in every row: ["exists", ["?m"], ["and", ["mother", "?c", "?m"], ["female", "?m"]]].
      Added rule-head-and capability786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • An invented value is an unknown, written ["some", "?m", ["mother", "ben", "?m"]]: the value ?m stands for in a row ["mother", "ben", ?m]. The form is ordinary Lion, and evaluating it gives the same unknown, so a program can write one, put it in a fact (["fact", ["tall", ["some", "?m", ["mother", "ben", "?m"]]]]), compare it, or look it up. Inside a rule, query, or find, some waits for the variables the rule binds, and every other variable of its goal is its own. With several variables in exists, each gets its own unknown, and its some mentions the others.
      Added some special-form786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • ["value/unknown?", x] is true for an unknown, so ["not", ["value/unknown?", "?m"]] keeps only known answers. value/object? is false for one.
      Added value/unknown? function786fdc0 existential-rules.json
    • why explains a row by an answer that gives it as it is, when one does, so after a key makes unknowns equal every row still rests only on rows explained before it. A row that a rule which invents gives only because a key or an equality rule made its unknown equal to another value ends with a new kind of premise, {"same": [unknown, value]}.
      Added why-same-premise capability786fdc0 existential-rules.json
    • Equality rules: a rule's head can be ["=", a, b], which says the two are one value whenever the body holds. While Lion derives the relations its body reads, an unknown a rule invented there takes the value on the other side, by the rule keys follow, so ["rule", ["=", "?m1", "?m2"], ["twin", "?a", "?b"], ["mother", "?a", "?m1"], ["mother", "?b", "?m2"]] gives twins one mother. The rule holds as the invariant ["and", goal, ..., ["not", ["=", a, b]]] too, so a rule that does not hold is not added and a change that leaves two different known values under it is refused, in an invariant's words. Lion follows each invented value through the columns of the rules, and the relations of a rule that invents an unknown an equality rule can meet are derived together with every relation the equality rule reads, so the unknown can pass through any number of derived relations first: with ["rule", ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], the rule ["rule", ["=", "?m", "?n"], ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["birth", "?c", "?n"]] makes ben's unknown mother the one his birth record names. A question about those relations, such as a goal under not, would go through recursion, and is refused when the rule is added, whatever the facts, with the message any such question gets: Rule [...] asks about "private", which depends on "listed". A question, such as a goal under "not", cannot go through recursion. A question about columns no invented value reaches is allowed. A head can join relation calls and = with and.

["string/slice", "lionlang", 0, 4] is "lion", and the two parts of a cut at any position join back into the whole. Like every library function, each waits for a logic variable and refuses a call with another number of arguments.

    • The lion-reasoning skill keeps the record of an experiment loop, in the manner of autoresearch. Notes declare scores, numbers to make better, such as {"question": {"comparisons": "bench.mjs"}, "better": "lower"}, and directions, the ideas to try; an observation that tries a direction is an experiment of it. What a version is sure to give is its worst run: the best is the best of those, and a version has improved a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to give, so improved, best, score_in, and regressed follow the evidence and not one lucky run; runs of a score that differ are its spread rather than a dispute. A direction pays off when its experiment improves a score, and is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, 3 unless it says. The standing question "Where should the next experiment go?" lists the live directions, those that paid off most first.

    • A lion-reasoning score can list what it requires, such as {"question": {"failing tests": "test.mjs"}, "value": 0}: a version where that is unanswered or answered otherwise has no score, and unmet lists it, so a change that breaks the tests never becomes the best. A direction can list what it needs; it waits while that is unanswered or not yet decided by whoever ask names, and is ruled_out once it is answered otherwise, so the user's answer prunes the directions.

    • A relation that rules invent rows of is derived in full, as an aggregated relation is, and so is a relation derived together with one because an equality rule reads it. A goal-directed query gives the same answers.
      Changed equality-group-relation-derivation is in-full logic Changed goal-directed-equality-group-relation is same-as-full logic Changed goal-directed-invented-relation is same-as-full logic Changed invented-relation-derivation is in-full logicexistential-rules.json 1d5800a 786fdc0
    • exists in a rule head says the head holds for values nobody has given, and the rule invents them: ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], ["person", "?c"]] gives every person a mother. A rule invents only for an answer whose head does not hold already, so with ["mother", "ada", "eve"] it invents nothing for ada. Rules that invent wait until every rule that invents nothing has finished; then every rule that invents, and whose head does not hold, invents, all at once; the other rules run on what was invented; and so on until nothing more is invented. So the result does not depend on the order rules or facts were added in. A rule that invents cannot aggregate: ... both aggregates and lists variables in "exists". A rule that invents values cannot aggregate.
      Changed existential-rule-aggregate is error logic Changed existential-rule-head-already-holds is invents-nothing logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md

    • The check that evaluation finishes is weak acyclicity, one rule for computed and invented values. Values flow from the columns a rule's body reads to the columns of its head, and a rule may make a new value for a column, by computing it or inventing it, as long as that value never flows back, through the rules, into making another. ["rule", ["b", "?x", ["number/add", "?x", 10]], ["a", "?x"]] with ["rule", ["a", "?x"], ["b", "?x", "?y"]] used to be refused, since any computed value in a recursive rule's head was, and is now accepted. Every program accepted before is still accepted. A computed value that flows back is refused with the same message as before. An invented one is refused with Rule [...] invents a value for "?m" in its head while recursing, which may never finish. Invent the value in a rule that does not recurse.

    • Equality rules: a rule's head can be ["=", a, b], which says the two are one value whenever the body holds. While Lion derives the relations its body reads, an unknown a rule invented there takes the value on the other side, by the rule keys follow, so ["rule", ["=", "?m1", "?m2"], ["twin", "?a", "?b"], ["mother", "?a", "?m1"], ["mother", "?b", "?m2"]] gives twins one mother. The rule holds as the invariant ["and", goal, ..., ["not", ["=", a, b]]] too, so a rule that does not hold is not added and a change that leaves two different known values under it is refused, in an invariant's words. Lion follows each invented value through the columns of the rules, and the relations of a rule that invents an unknown an equality rule can meet are derived together with every relation the equality rule reads, so the unknown can pass through any number of derived relations first: with ["rule", ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], the rule ["rule", ["=", "?m", "?n"], ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["birth", "?c", "?n"]] makes ben's unknown mother the one his birth record names. A question about those relations, such as a goal under not, would go through recursion, and is refused when the rule is added, whatever the facts, with the message any such question gets: Rule [...] asks about "private", which depends on "listed". A question, such as a goal under "not", cannot go through recursion. A question about columns no invented value reaches is allowed. A head can join relation calls and = with and.

    • Goal-directed queries are no longer hundreds of times slower than full evaluation on a large model asked many questions. A goal that knows none of its arguments now reads the relation itself, which the database derives once and keeps for every later query, instead of each query deriving a copy that holds every row anyway; a query that knows an argument of a relation the database already holds in full looks its rows up there; and a rule whose known argument sits inside a record pattern or a schema, such as ["claim", "?c", ["schema/open", {"topic": "?t"}]], runs as written and keeps the rows asked about, instead of scanning claim once for each value asked about. On the research model of Lion's own development, the 37 questions of its page took 36.6 seconds goal-directed and 0.12 seconds in full; they now take 0.11 seconds goal-directed. A host no longer needs new LogicDatabase({ goalDirected: false }) for such a model.

    Fixed 10

    • Goal-directed queries are no longer hundreds of times slower than full evaluation on a large model asked many questions. A goal that knows none of its arguments now reads the relation itself, which the database derives once and keeps for every later query, instead of each query deriving a copy that holds every row anyway; a query that knows an argument of a relation the database already holds in full looks its rows up there; and a rule whose known argument sits inside a record pattern or a schema, such as ["claim", "?c", ["schema/open", {"topic": "?t"}]], runs as written and keeps the rows asked about, instead of scanning claim once for each value asked about. On the research model of Lion's own development, the 37 questions of its page took 36.6 seconds goal-directed and 0.12 seconds in full; they now take 0.11 seconds goal-directed. A host no longer needs new LogicDatabase({ goalDirected: false }) for such a model.
      Fixed goal-directed-goal-knowing-no-arguments is reads-shared-relation, was derives-full-copy logic Fixed goal-directed-known-argument-in-pattern is runs-as-written, was scans-per-value logic Fixed goal-directed-known-argument-relation-held-in-full is looked-up-in-held-rows logic Fixed goal-directed-large-model-many-questions-speed is like-full-evaluation, was hundreds-of-times-slower logicWhy Goal-directed queries share what is derived in full, and a relation is derived when a goal first reads itgoal-directed-shares-full-relations-changes.json
    • A research page sends Lion one question at a time, so a question's time limit counts its own run and not its wait behind the others: on Lion's own research model two of the page's questions used to stop at the limit. build-explorer.mjs indexes each source's text once, not once per quote: building that page took 73 seconds and takes one.

    Decided 26

    • exists in a rule head says the head holds for values nobody has given, and the rule invents them: ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], ["person", "?c"]] gives every person a mother. A rule invents only for an answer whose head does not hold already, so with ["mother", "ada", "eve"] it invents nothing for ada. Rules that invent wait until every rule that invents nothing has finished; then every rule that invents, and whose head does not hold, invents, all at once; the other rules run on what was invented; and so on until nothing more is invented. So the result does not depend on the order rules or facts were added in. A rule that invents cannot aggregate: ... both aggregates and lists variables in "exists". A rule that invents values cannot aggregate.
      Decided chase-strategy: restricted-datalog-first-parallel, because the result does not depend on the order of rules or facts logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json
    • The check that evaluation finishes is weak acyclicity, one rule for computed and invented values. Values flow from the columns a rule's body reads to the columns of its head, and a rule may make a new value for a column, by computing it or inventing it, as long as that value never flows back, through the rules, into making another. ["rule", ["b", "?x", ["number/add", "?x", 10]], ["a", "?x"]] with ["rule", ["a", "?x"], ["b", "?x", "?y"]] used to be refused, since any computed value in a recursive rule's head was, and is now accepted. Every program accepted before is still accepted. A computed value that flows back is refused with the same message as before. An invented one is refused with Rule [...] invents a value for "?m" in its head while recursing, which may never finish. Invent the value in a rule that does not recurse.
      Decided termination-check: weak-acyclicity over no-computed-values-in-recursion, because one rule for computed and invented values, which accepts every program the old check did, and more, was no-computed-values-in-recursion logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json

      Decided equality-generating-dependencies: equality-rule-head over keys-only, because it gives the general form, built from what Lion already has rather than beside it logicb030d8a

    Rules 28

    • An unknown is data, as a string is: rows, facts, answers, finds, and aggregates hold it. It equals itself and nothing else, and two unknowns are the same when they are written the same way. It sorts after every record, and unknowns sort by how they are written. A function that needs a number or a string fails on one, as it does on any value of the wrong kind. Lion stays closed-world: ["not", ["=", "?m", "eve"]] holds for ben's unknown mother.
      Rules closed-world Lion stays closed-world: not holds for anything that is not known, unknowns included logic Rules unknowns-are-data An unknown is data, equal only to itself, and sorts after records; two unknowns are the same when written the same way logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • exists in a rule head says the head holds for values nobody has given, and the rule invents them: ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], ["person", "?c"]] gives every person a mother. A rule invents only for an answer whose head does not hold already, so with ["mother", "ada", "eve"] it invents nothing for ada. Rules that invent wait until every rule that invents nothing has finished; then every rule that invents, and whose head does not hold, invents, all at once; the other rules run on what was invented; and so on until nothing more is invented. So the result does not depend on the order rules or facts were added in. A rule that invents cannot aggregate: ... both aggregates and lists variables in "exists". A rule that invents values cannot aggregate.
      Rules datalog-first-parallel-chase Rules that invent wait until the others are done, then every one whose head does not hold invents at once, so the result does not depend on the order of rules or facts logic Rules restricted-chase A rule invents only for an answer whose head does not hold already logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • A key makes unknowns equal. When two rows of a keyed relation have the same key and differ only where one holds an unknown that a rule of the keyed relation, or of a relation in a recursive cycle with it, invented, the unknown takes the other row's value: a given value, or, when both are such unknowns, the one that sorts first. With {"key": "child"} on mother, "everyone has a mother" and "twins share a mother" give twins ben and cy the one unknown mother ["some", "?m", ["mother", "ben", "?m"]]. Two different given values are still an error, with the key's message, and an unknown that a fact holds is given, so a key never changes it. An unknown never takes a value that describes it, so of two invented unknowns where one describes the other, the one that describes takes the other.
      Rules keys-make-unknowns-equal Two rows of a keyed relation that differ only in unknowns the group invented are made one: the given value or the unknown that sorts first stays, an unknown never takes a value that describes it, and two given values are still an error logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json README.md
    • Negative constraints are invariants, as before.
      Rules negative-constraints-are-invariants Datalog± negative constraints are Lion's invariants logic786fdc0
    • The check that evaluation finishes is weak acyclicity, one rule for computed and invented values. Values flow from the columns a rule's body reads to the columns of its head, and a rule may make a new value for a column, by computing it or inventing it, as long as that value never flows back, through the rules, into making another. ["rule", ["b", "?x", ["number/add", "?x", 10]], ["a", "?x"]] with ["rule", ["a", "?x"], ["b", "?x", "?y"]] used to be refused, since any computed value in a recursive rule's head was, and is now accepted. Every program accepted before is still accepted. A computed value that flows back is refused with the same message as before. An invented one is refused with Rule [...] invents a value for "?m" in its head while recursing, which may never finish. Invent the value in a rule that does not recurse.
      Rules recursion-cannot-compute-values A recursive rule cannot compute new values for its head columns, in the head itself or through = or in, so evaluation always finishes logic Rules weak-acyclicity A rule may make a new value for a column, by computing or inventing it, as long as that value never flows back through the rules into making another logic786fdc0 existential-rules.json 1d5800a README.md
    • Equality rules: a rule's head can be ["=", a, b], which says the two are one value whenever the body holds. While Lion derives the relations its body reads, an unknown a rule invented there takes the value on the other side, by the rule keys follow, so ["rule", ["=", "?m1", "?m2"], ["twin", "?a", "?b"], ["mother", "?a", "?m1"], ["mother", "?b", "?m2"]] gives twins one mother. The rule holds as the invariant ["and", goal, ..., ["not", ["=", a, b]]] too, so a rule that does not hold is not added and a change that leaves two different known values under it is refused, in an invariant's words. Lion follows each invented value through the columns of the rules, and the relations of a rule that invents an unknown an equality rule can meet are derived together with every relation the equality rule reads, so the unknown can pass through any number of derived relations first: with ["rule", ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], the rule ["rule", ["=", "?m", "?n"], ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["birth", "?c", "?n"]] makes ben's unknown mother the one his birth record names. A question about those relations, such as a goal under not, would go through recursion, and is refused when the rule is added, whatever the facts, with the message any such question gets: Rule [...] asks about "private", which depends on "listed". A question, such as a goal under "not", cannot go through recursion. A question about columns no invented value reaches is allowed. A head can join relation calls and = with and.
      Rules equality-merges-like-keys An equality rule makes an unknown the rules invented take the value on the other side, by the same rule keys follow logic Rules equality-rule-is-invariant An equality rule holds as the invariant it stands for, as a relation's schema holds as its invariant: a rule that does not hold is not added, and a change that leaves two different known values under it is refused logicb030d8a existential-rules.json README.md
    • Goal-directed queries are no longer hundreds of times slower than full evaluation on a large model asked many questions. A goal that knows none of its arguments now reads the relation itself, which the database derives once and keeps for every later query, instead of each query deriving a copy that holds every row anyway; a query that knows an argument of a relation the database already holds in full looks its rows up there; and a rule whose known argument sits inside a record pattern or a schema, such as ["claim", "?c", ["schema/open", {"topic": "?t"}]], runs as written and keeps the rows asked about, instead of scanning claim once for each value asked about. On the research model of Lion's own development, the 37 questions of its page took 36.6 seconds goal-directed and 0.12 seconds in full; they now take 0.11 seconds goal-directed. A host no longer needs new LogicDatabase({ goalDirected: false }) for such a model.
      Rules goal-directed-shares-full-relations A goal-directed query derives a copy only of what it knows an argument of, and shares every relation derived in full with later queries logicRecord Goal-directed queries share what is derived in full, and a relation is derived when a goal first reads itWhy Goal-directed queries share what is derived in full, and a relation is derived when a goal first reads itgoal-directed-shares-full-relations.json goal-directed-shares-full-relations-changes.json
    • A relation is derived the first time a goal reads it with an answer to extend, in goal-directed and full evaluation alike, so a query never fails on a relation that no answer reaches. With ["rule", ["report", "?t"], ["audit", "?t"], ["broken", "?t"]] and no audit rows, ["query", ["report", "?t"]] gives [] even when deriving broken would fail; it used to derive broken before running the rule, and fail.

    • The lion-research skill records leads, the lines of inquiry a research run follows: "leads": [{"id": "outside-warehouses", "statement": "…", "pursues": [{"warehouses": "tarnwell"}], "patience": 2}], and "for": ["outside-warehouses"] on each source read to follow one. A source pays off for a lead when it says something first-hand the lead covers; a lead is done when every question it pursues has an answer two publishers give first-hand, waits while the reader has not chosen a sense of one, and is set aside after as many sources in a row as its patience gave it nothing. The standing questions ask where the next search should go and how each lead ended, and the page's "How solid is it" shows the reader "What was looked for".
      Rules lead-done-when-confirmed A research lead is done when every question it pursues has an answer two publishers give first-hand skills Rules patience-since-last-payoff A direction or a lead is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, counted since its last payoff skillsRecord A research lead is done when every question it pursues has an answer two publishers give first-hand A direction or a lead is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, counted since its last payoffWhy A research lead is done when every question it pursues has an answer two publishers give first-hand A direction or a lead is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, counted since its last payoff A version improves a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to givelead-done-when-confirmed.json skill-autoresearch.json patience-since-last-payoff.json
    • The research page check's last entry says how to fix what it lists: Questions the plan names that a choice set aside, or that have readings nobody chose between. This must be empty: reach each through meant, or ask the reader which sense they mean. build-explorer.mjs reminds the agent to run it whenever the plan names questions as records, and the skill says the check must give [].
      Rules research-page-check-empty The research page check must give [] skillsskill-autoresearch.json
    • The lion-reasoning skill keeps the record of an experiment loop, in the manner of autoresearch. Notes declare scores, numbers to make better, such as {"question": {"comparisons": "bench.mjs"}, "better": "lower"}, and directions, the ideas to try; an observation that tries a direction is an experiment of it. What a version is sure to give is its worst run: the best is the best of those, and a version has improved a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to give, so improved, best, score_in, and regressed follow the evidence and not one lucky run; runs of a score that differ are its spread rather than a dispute. A direction pays off when its experiment improves a score, and is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, 3 unless it says. The standing question "Where should the next experiment go?" lists the live directions, those that paid off most first.
      Rules score-improves-past-noise A version improves a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to give skillsRecord A version improves a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to giveWhy A direction or a lead is set aside after as many misses in a row as its patience, counted since its last payoff A version improves a score when its worst run beats the best that any earlier version was sure to givescore-improves-past-noise.json skill-autoresearch.json
    • A lion-reasoning score can list what it requires, such as {"question": {"failing tests": "test.mjs"}, "value": 0}: a version where that is unanswered or answered otherwise has no score, and unmet lists it, so a change that breaks the tests never becomes the best. A direction can list what it needs; it waits while that is unanswered or not yet decided by whoever ask names, and is ruled_out once it is answered otherwise, so the user's answer prunes the directions.

    • Goal-directed queries are no longer hundreds of times slower than full evaluation on a large model asked many questions. A goal that knows none of its arguments now reads the relation itself, which the database derives once and keeps for every later query, instead of each query deriving a copy that holds every row anyway; a query that knows an argument of a relation the database already holds in full looks its rows up there; and a rule whose known argument sits inside a record pattern or a schema, such as ["claim", "?c", ["schema/open", {"topic": "?t"}]], runs as written and keeps the rows asked about, instead of scanning claim once for each value asked about. On the research model of Lion's own development, the 37 questions of its page took 36.6 seconds goal-directed and 0.12 seconds in full; they now take 0.11 seconds goal-directed. A host no longer needs new LogicDatabase({ goalDirected: false }) for such a model.

    lion-reasoning skill

    No package changed. skills/lion-reasoning is a new agent skill that uses Lion as the working memory of an agent's reasoning while it works, and the README has a section on it.

    • 18 Added
    • 25 Changed
    • 1 Decided
    • 7 Rules
    • 19 Figures
    70 changes

    Added 18

    • The skill. An agent records what it observed, each observation a question and a value with the words of a command's output or a file that show it, and what it believes, each belief with the answers it predicts. A problem is a question with the value that shows it. Rules derive what the agent would otherwise have to remember to check.
      Added lion-reasoning skill2026-11-13-lion-reasoning-skill.json 4c8df1b README.md
    • Properties in packages/metrics check the core program against a plain model of versions, evidence, and beliefs, rival explanations against the law that an answer keeps exactly those that predicted it, the recorder, the versions against the files they were taken from, and the chain from changing files to the present answer. Fifteen mutations break those behaviors, and mutation.ts takes a package so a mutation can run the tests of metrics.
      Added mutation-package-option option2026-11-13-lion-reasoning-skill.json 4c8df1b README.md
    • scripts/start.mjs, see.mjs, record.mjs, replay.mjs, and ask.mjs. see.mjs runs a command and keeps its output and exit status as evidence, with the hash of what it depends on when it ran. record.mjs writes a step from plain notes, refuses a quote that is not in the text it came from, and stamps each belief with the version it was formed in. Every version of the project is kept as the changes since the last. The scripts run the published @lionlang/cli, so changing Lion itself never changes the checker, and a question runs on a copy of the model.
      Added reasoning-ask-mjs tool Added reasoning-replay-mjs tool Added reasoning-see-mjs tool Added reasoning-start-mjs toolWhy A belief is judged by the evidence of every version from the one it was formed in on, and an explanation by the versions where its problem shows The skills' scripts run the published @lionlang/cli, never the copy of Lion in the project2026-11-13-lion-reasoning-skill.json 4c8df1b README.md
    • assets/core.json, the program every model starts from. Each observation speaks for the versions of the project in which the files it depends on hold what they held when it was seen, so evidence about a changed file is stale and changed lists what the work changed. What the agent ran or read overrules what it was told or recalled, and overruled lists each time. A belief is contradicted, borne out, or untested by the evidence of every version from the one it was formed in on, and a belief that explains a problem by the versions where the problem shows, so a fix does not count against the explanation of the bug it fixed. For rival explanations, decisive names the questions they answer differently, remaining the ones still standing, settled the one left when all its predictions are borne out, and unexplained a problem with none left. needed and open say what the task must still observe.

    Changed during the first trial

    Two agents fixed one real bug in history-free copies of Lion from before commit 28ae742: loading special-forms/lambda first crashed with "Cannot access 'evaluateLambda' before initialization". One used the skill and one did not. Both found the same cause and the same 11 of 49 modules, and both fixes were verified independently: no module fails when loaded first, the core tests and typecheck pass, and each new test fails on the old code. The cost was the same within noise: 238,607 tokens, 81 tool calls, and 17.5 minutes with the skill; 235,018 tokens, 88 tool calls, and 18.3 minutes without. The skill's agent put 30 to 35% of its effort into the model. The model caught one thing that changed what it did: its "fails on the old code" evidence was stale after a later edit to the test, so it ran the check again. It reported five problems with the skill, each fixed above:

    lion-research skill

    No package changed. skills/lion-research is a new agent skill that uses Lion as the working memory of a deep research run, and the README has a section on it.

    • 18 Added
    • 39 Changed
    • 2 Decided
    • 5 Rules
    • 14 Figures
    78 changes

    Added 18

    • The skill. An agent records what each source says as facts, each with the quote that carries it, and writes rules that derive its conclusions, so the model is a materialized view of the research. Its assumptions are rules that the evidence can contradict. A run ends with the saved model and one page for the person who asked for the research.
      Added lion-research skill2026-11-13-lion-research-skill.json 284f00f README.md
    • backing lists the publishers behind each answer
      Added research-backing capabilityRecord The research skill counts the publishers who give an answer first-hand, not the sources that state itresearch-counts-publishers.json
    • scripts/build-explorer.mjs, which packs a model and the plan of its page into one HTML file with the evaluator inside it. The page is for a reader who does not know Lion, and it has no fixed form: the agent writes a plan, page.json, for what this reader wants to know. A plan names the views and fills each with blocks: an answer in plain words with its evidence under it, key figures, a table, a timeline, a comparison grid, a lookup whose answer changes as the reader chooses from lists, how solid the findings are, the sources, and text. The plan states no facts: its summary, answers, notes, and figures are Lion expressions that the page evaluates against the model each time it opens, so the wording follows the model and a cond on disputed or corroborated picks the sentence. A lookup's query is a Lion function, called with what the reader chose as data. assets/words.json gives the expressions functions for wording: a list as a sentence lists it, a number with separators, a count with its noun. The trust block is built from the core: what independent publishers confirm, where sources disagree, what rests on one publisher's word, what is second-hand, what was misquoted, and which assumptions held. The query editor and the model's tables are always the last view, for readers who know Lion, where a query can also add facts to ask what would follow. The script also writes every query the plan asks as one Lion record, so they can all be run before the page is opened.
      Added research-build-explorer-mjs tool Added research-page-json fileWhy Text built on Lion is computed by Lion expressions, not filled into a template, and a helper any program would want goes into the standard library2026-11-13-lion-research-skill.json 284f00f README.md

    • assets/core.json, the program every research model starts from. It says who stands behind each answer: the publishers who give it first-hand, in a claim credited to nobody else. Sources with one publisher are one voice, and a source that relays another adds nothing, so an answer that three articles took from one press release rests on one publisher. It derives which answers independent publishers confirm, which rest on one publisher's word and how many on each, which are known only second-hand, which sources are credited with something they do not say, which questions sources dispute, which credited sources are unread, and which assumptions hold. Its invariants reject a claim without a known source.

The page is for a reader who does not know Lion, and it has no fixed form: the agent writes a plan, page.json, for what this reader wants to know. A plan names the views and fills each with blocks: an answer in plain words with its evidence under it, key figures, a table, a timeline, a comparison grid, a lookup whose answer changes as the reader chooses from lists, how solid the findings are, the sources, and text. The plan states no facts: its summary, answers, notes, and figures are Lion expressions that the page evaluates against the model each time it opens, so the wording follows the model and a cond on disputed or corroborated picks the sentence. A lookup's query is a Lion function, called with what the reader chose as data. assets/words.json gives the expressions functions for wording: a list as a sentence lists it, a number with separators, a count with its noun. The trust block is built from the core: what independent publishers confirm, where sources disagree, what rests on one publisher's word, what is second-hand, what was misquoted, and which assumptions held. The query editor and the model's tables are always the last view, for readers who know Lion, where a query can also add facts to ask what would follow. The script also writes every query the plan asks as one Lion record, so they can all be run before the page is opened.

    Changed during the first trial

    A trial run researched the Microsoft 365 outage of 12 November 2026 with the first version of the skill: 19 sources and 175 claims. That version's core followed each claim to the source it was credited to and counted distinct sources. On the trial's model it called 15 answers corroborated. Eight of them were not: two channels of one company counted as two origins in three, two articles from one newspaper in one, and in four an origin was a source that was only credited, either unread or saying something else. The core above replaced it. On the same evidence it calls 7 answers corroborated, the 7 the trial's agent reached with stricter rules of its own, and it reports 4 misquotes and 26 answers known only second-hand.

    • "On this page" marks the section a link was followed to. For every one of the page's 273 section links it used to mark the section before, or none for a document's first section: a link puts a heading 168 pixels below the top of the window, the page's scroll padding and the heading's scroll margin together, and a heading counted as reached only above 140. A section now counts as reached where a link puts its heading, read from the stylesheet. At the end of a page the last section is the one being read, where its heading could never get high enough to be marked, as in 29 of the 39 documents in a window 800 pixels tall. A section a link was followed to stays marked for as long as the page stays where the link left it, also when the page is too short to bring its heading up.

    Decided 1

    • "On this page" marks the section a link was followed to. For every one of the page's 273 section links it used to mark the section before, or none for a document's first section: a link puts a heading 168 pixels below the top of the window, the page's scroll padding and the heading's scroll margin together, and a heading counted as reached only above 140. A section now counts as reached where a link puts its heading, read from the stylesheet. At the end of a page the last section is the one being read, where its heading could never get high enough to be marked, as in 29 of the 39 documents in a window 800 pixels tall. A section a link was followed to stays marked for as long as the page stays where the link left it, also when the page is too short to bring its heading up.
      Decided toc-section-reached: where-link-puts-heading over fixed-140-px, because a link puts a heading 168 px below the top of the window, and a heading counted as reached only above a fixed 140 px site2026-11-13-lionlang-dev.json faed4c4

    @lionlang/core 0.7.0 @lionlang/cli 0.6.0

    Schemas say what a value must be, and one rule says what fits: whatever checks a value against a schema asks whether the value fits it. A logic variable in a schema is the value it meets, so a schema is also a pattern that takes data apart.

    Rules 9

    • The README says what Lion does where the research model found it said otherwise. A cond condition counts as false when it is false, null, 0, or "", as the reference's truthiness rule already said, where the README said every string counts as true. A question in plain code is asked as soon as something needs its value, and a program or begin whose value is a goal gives the goal as written, so ["exists", ["?y"], ["=", "?y", 1]] is true as a value, as in ["value/identity", …], and not as a program; the reference says the same. The empty array [] evaluates to itself. The editor section no longer describes the outline, inspector, and source views it lost, its command is turbo dev --filter=@lionlang/repl, and the link to the agent's program no longer points into a local folder. AGENTS.md says bun run test, and packages/examples/CLAUDE.md says the tests use Vitest, as AGENTS.md does.

    • Equality rules: a rule's head can be ["=", a, b], which says the two are one value whenever the body holds. While Lion derives the relations its body reads, an unknown a rule invented there takes the value on the other side, by the rule keys follow, so ["rule", ["=", "?m1", "?m2"], ["twin", "?a", "?b"], ["mother", "?a", "?m1"], ["mother", "?b", "?m2"]] gives twins one mother. The rule holds as the invariant ["and", goal, ..., ["not", ["=", a, b]]] too, so a rule that does not hold is not added and a change that leaves two different known values under it is refused, in an invariant's words. Lion follows each invented value through the columns of the rules, and the relations of a rule that invents an unknown an equality rule can meet are derived together with every relation the equality rule reads, so the unknown can pass through any number of derived relations first: with ["rule", ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], the rule ["rule", ["=", "?m", "?n"], ["listed", "?c", "?m"], ["birth", "?c", "?n"]] makes ben's unknown mother the one his birth record names. A question about those relations, such as a goal under not, would go through recursion, and is refused when the rule is added, whatever the facts, with the message any such question gets: Rule [...] asks about "private", which depends on "listed". A question, such as a goal under "not", cannot go through recursion. A question about columns no invented value reaches is allowed. A head can join relation calls and = with and.

    • Goal-directed queries. A query that gives a rule-defined relation a known argument, such as ["path", "a", "?to"], now runs a magic-sets rewrite of the rules, so evaluation derives only the facts the query can reach instead of every fact the program implies. A query along a 3,000-node chain that would otherwise derive about 4.5 million paths returns in milliseconds. Aggregated, computed, and negated relations are still computed in full, answers match full evaluation, and new LogicDatabase({ goalDirected: false }) turns the rewrite off. lionlang.dev has a live Goal-directed queries card.

    • Recursion through lattice aggregates. aggregate/min, aggregate/max, and the new aggregate/shortest and aggregate/union only move one way, so a recursive rule can aggregate with them and compute the aggregated value, which makes minimum distances and shortest paths expressible.     • The README says what Lion does where the research model found it said otherwise. A cond condition counts as false when it is false, null, 0, or "", as the reference's truthiness rule already said, where the README said every string counts as true. A question in plain code is asked as soon as something needs its value, and a program or begin whose value is a goal gives the goal as written, so ["exists", ["?y"], ["=", "?y", 1]] is true as a value, as in ["value/identity", …], and not as a program; the reference says the same. The empty array [] evaluates to itself. The editor section no longer describes the outline, inspector, and source views it lost, its command is turbo dev --filter=@lionlang/repl, and the link to the agent's program no longer points into a local folder. AGENTS.md says bun run test, and packages/examples/CLAUDE.md says the tests use Vitest, as AGENTS.md does.

    Decided 29

    • Every commit runs the tests and the formatter, and CI checks every pull request and push to main
      Decided quality-gates: pre-commit-hook-and-ci over unchecked, because nothing ran the tests or a formatter before a commit or after a push buildRecord Every commit runs the tests and the formatter, and CI checks every pull request and push to mainquality-gates.json
    • The README says what Lion does where the research model found it said otherwise. A cond condition counts as false when it is false, null, 0, or "", as the reference's truthiness rule already said, where the README said every string counts as true. A question in plain code is asked as soon as something needs its value, and a program or begin whose value is a goal gives the goal as written, so ["exists", ["?y"], ["=", "?y", 1]] is true as a value, as in ["value/identity", …], and not as a program; the reference says the same. The empty array [] evaluates to itself. The editor section no longer describes the outline, inspector, and source views it lost, its command is turbo dev --filter=@lionlang/repl, and the link to the agent's program no longer points into a local folder. AGENTS.md says bun run test, and packages/examples/CLAUDE.md says the tests use Vitest, as AGENTS.md does.
      Decided test-command: bun-run-test processRecord Every commit runs the tests and the formatter, and CI checks every pull request and push to mainb60f4a1 quality-gates.json research-model.json AGENTS.md

    Breaking 3

    • Where JavaScript and JSON disagree, Lion follows JSON, everywhere the case comes up. Arithmetic whose result is not a finite number, such as division by zero or an overflow, fails with the new ArithmeticError

    • The README says what Lion does where the research model found it said otherwise. A cond condition counts as false when it is false, null, 0, or "", as the reference's truthiness rule already said, where the README said every string counts as true. A question in plain code is asked as soon as something needs its value, and a program or begin whose value is a goal gives the goal as written, so ["exists", ["?y"], ["=", "?y", 1]] is true as a value, as in ["value/identity", …], and not as a program; the reference says the same. The empty array [] evaluates to itself. The editor section no longer describes the outline, inspector, and source views it lost, its command is turbo dev --filter=@lionlang/repl, and the link to the agent's program no longer points into a local folder. AGENTS.md says bun run test, and packages/examples/CLAUDE.md says the tests use Vitest, as AGENTS.md does.

    • The README says what Lion does where the research model found it said otherwise. A cond condition counts as false when it is false, null, 0, or "", as the reference's truthiness rule already said, where the README said every string counts as true. A question in plain code is asked as soon as something needs its value, and a program or begin whose value is a goal gives the goal as written, so ["exists", ["?y"], ["=", "?y", 1]] is true as a value, as in ["value/identity", …], and not as a program; the reference says the same. The empty array [] evaluates to itself. The editor section no longer describes the outline, inspector, and source views it lost, its command is turbo dev --filter=@lionlang/repl, and the link to the agent's program no longer points into a local folder. AGENTS.md says bun run test, and packages/examples/CLAUDE.md says the tests use Vitest, as AGENTS.md does.
